reference_text:
Welcome to the course. We will work through each concept carefully, connect the
ideas step by step, and use practical examples to make technical topics easier
to understand. When we introduce a new method, focus first on the problem it
solves and why it is useful. For example, in machine learning, features are the
information we give the model, while the target is what we want it to predict.
Now consider a simple question: what changes when the data contains missing
values? We will think through the reason and then look at the code. In Python,
we can inspect the data, run one small step at a time, and explain what the
result means. The goal is to understand the logic, not simply memorize syntax.

slides.title: Data Cleaning in PostgreSQL
slides.transcript:
Welcome to Module 9, Data Cleaning in Postgres.

Before we start, think about how much SQL you can already use. In the earlier modules, you learned how relational databases organize data, how to query tables with S Q L, how to aggregate values, apply logical conditions, join related tables, and use subqueries. In the previous module, you also worked with strings and dates, including functions that help us transform text and handle date values.

[tts-break]

Now we will bring many of those skills together for a very practical problem: real data is rarely clean. A customer name may contain extra spaces. An email may use inconsistent capitalization. A phone number may contain parentheses, spaces, or dashes. Some values may be missing, invalid, or duplicated.

The goal is not simply to make the data look nicer. Our goal is to profile the data, preserve the original evidence, standardize values when we understand the rule, validate what we can, identify duplicates, and make changes safely. By the end of this module, I want you to think of data cleaning as a careful and explainable process rather than a collection of quick fixes.

slides.title: Data Cleaning Is Evidence-Based Decision Making
slides.transcript:
A useful way to think about data cleaning is as evidence-based decision making.

We begin by observing what is actually in the data. Before changing anything, count missing values, blank strings, invalid values, duplicates, and unusual values. We want to understand the problem before we try to solve it.

[tts-break]

Next, we decide what can be standardized using a documented rule. For example, if an email has extra spaces around it, removing those spaces does not change the meaning of the email address. That is a reasonable standardization.

But we should also preserve the original evidence. A cleaned value is our interpretation of the source value. It should not erase where the value came from.

And finally, when we do not know the correct answer, we should not guess. A suspicious record can be flagged for review instead of being automatically changed. That mindset will guide the entire module.

slides.title: Invalid Does Not Mean Replace with Something Plausible
slides.transcript:
One of the most important ideas in data cleaning is that an invalid value does not automatically tell us what the correct value should be.

Suppose a product price is negative fifty dollars. We can easily use an absolute value function and turn negative fifty into positive fifty. Technically, that is easy. But do we actually know that fifty dollars is the correct price? Maybe the negative number represents a refund. Maybe the source system has an error. Maybe the intended value was five hundred.

[tts-break]

So the safer response is to flag the value as invalid and investigate the source or the business rule.

This distinction is important. Data cleaning should reduce inconsistency without inventing facts. Whenever you are tempted to automatically fix a suspicious value, ask yourself one question: do I have evidence for the replacement, or am I only choosing something that looks reasonable?

slides.title: What You Should Be Able to Do
slides.transcript:
By the end of this module, you should be able to perform several connected data-cleaning tasks with S Q L.

First, you should be able to profile a dataset. That means measuring missing values, blanks, placeholders, invalid values, and possible duplicates.

Second, you should be able to standardize representations. For example, you may normalize names, email addresses, phone numbers, or categories without pretending that an uncertain value is known.

[tts-break]

You should also be able to validate values using clear rules, identify duplicate groups, and apply an explicit rule when choosing a preferred record.

Finally, you should know how to protect the original data. We will use views, transactions, returning results from updates, and database constraints.

The larger goal is not just to write working SQL. You should be able to explain why each cleaning decision is reasonable and what uncertainty still remains.

slides.title: A Practical Cleaning Cycle
slides.transcript:
A practical cleaning workflow can be organized into six steps.

First, profile the data. Measure the problems before changing anything.

Second, preserve the source. Keep the raw evidence available so you can always compare a cleaned result with its original value.

Third, normalize representations that have a known meaning. For example, trimming extra spaces is usually a safe normalization.

[tts-break]

Fourth, validate values against documented rules. Fifth, resolve problems that require a decision, such as duplicate records or rows that should be quarantined for review.

And sixth, prevent the same problems from appearing again. Once a rule is stable and well understood, we may enforce it with constraints or validation during data entry.

Notice the order. Prevention comes after we understand the data and the rules. Good cleaning is a cycle of measuring, deciding, checking, and improving.

slides.title: Cleaned Fields Should Remain Explainable
slides.transcript:
A cleaned value should be easy to explain.

Consider a customer name stored as Jane Smith with several extra spaces around it. A cleaned version can remove those spaces and use consistent capitalization. The same idea applies to an email address. We can remove surrounding spaces and convert the text to lowercase. For a phone number, we may remove punctuation and keep only the digits.

[tts-break]

These are useful analytical representations, but the original values still matter. If someone asks how a cleaned value was produced, we should be able to point back to the source and describe the transformation.

This is called preserving lineage or provenance. It means keeping enough information to reproduce and audit the cleaning process.

When possible, think in terms of two layers: what the source actually contained, and what representation we created for analysis.

slides.title: The Sample Data Contains Quality Problems
slides.transcript:
For this module, the sample database intentionally contains messy data so that we can practice realistic cleaning decisions.

The customers table includes missing values, blank text, inconsistent names, different phone formats, inconsistent email formatting, and possible duplicate identities.

The products table includes inconsistent category labels, invalid prices, and stock problems.

[tts-break]

The messy customers table acts more like a staging table. It contains mixed date formats, an invalid date, empty values, and a duplicate record. We will use it later to build a more complete cleaning pipeline.

The orders table gives us additional relational context.

As you work through the examples, do not think of these problems as unusual. Real operational databases often contain exactly this kind of variation, especially when information comes from multiple systems, manual entry, spreadsheets, or older applications.

slides.title: Inspect Raw Records First
slides.transcript:
Before writing cleaning logic, look at the raw records.

The query on the screen selects the customer identifier, name, email, phone, address, and signup date. It then orders the records by identifier.

When you run it, do not immediately start fixing values. First, look carefully.

[tts-break]

Can you see names with extra spaces? Are some names capitalized differently? Do phone numbers use different formats? Are there blank values that are different from null values? Do two rows look as if they may represent the same customer?

This first inspection gives you context. It is similar to opening a spreadsheet and scanning the columns before writing a transformation.

Later, we will automate much of this profiling, but visual inspection is still useful because it helps you understand what kinds of problems your SQL needs to detect.

slides.title: Begin with Counts and Distributions
slides.transcript:
After visually inspecting the data, start measuring it.

There are several questions we can ask. For missingness, how many values are null, and how many contain only blank text?

For validity, how many values violate a documented rule? For example, how many product prices are zero or negative?

For uniqueness, how many possible duplicate groups appear after we normalize the fields used for matching?

[tts-break]

And for distribution, are there values that are unusual enough to deserve investigation?

Imagine a dataset of patient ages. An age of ninety-five may be unusual but completely valid. An age of nine hundred fifty is almost certainly a problem.

The important idea is that unusual does not automatically mean invalid. Profiling helps us find where to look. Business knowledge and documented rules help us decide what the values mean.

slides.title: Non-Null and Non-Blank Counts
slides.transcript:
Here we are comparing two different questions.

The count function applied directly to a column counts values that are not null. But a text value containing an empty string or only spaces is still technically not null.

So we also create a nonblank version of the count. The query trims spaces from the text and uses the null if function to convert an empty result to null before counting it.

[tts-break]

For example, suppose a table has ten customer names. Eight rows contain visible names, one row contains null, and one row contains only spaces. A simple non-null count would report nine. A nonblank count would report eight.

That difference is useful because it tells us that missingness can be represented in more than one way.

When you run the query, compare the non-null and nonblank counts for the name, email, and phone columns.

slides.title: Different Missing States
slides.transcript:
Missing data does not always appear in the same form.

A null value means no SQL value is stored. A blank string is different. It is still a text value, but it contains no useful visible information.

You may also encounter sentinel values such as ten zeros in a phone field. A system may use that value to mean unknown or not provided.

[tts-break]

Another example is the literal word Unknown. That is not a null value. It is an actual category value that communicates uncertainty.

Why does this matter? Because we should not automatically treat all of these states as equivalent. Their meanings depend on the system and the business rules.

Before standardizing missing data, identify how missingness is represented and document which representations are allowed to be converted to null.

slides.title: Classify Phone States Explicitly
slides.transcript:
This query classifies phone values instead of immediately changing them.

The case expression first checks whether the phone is null. Then it checks whether the value becomes empty after trimming spaces. Next, it removes everything except digits and checks for known placeholder values, such as a phone number made entirely of zeros or nines.

Anything else is labeled as a candidate value.

[tts-break]

Notice the word candidate. We have not proven that the phone number is correct. We have only determined that it is not obviously missing, blank, or one of our known sentinel values.

For example, a ten-digit number can still belong to the wrong person. Technical validation and real-world correctness are different questions.

Run the query and compare the phone value with the state assigned to it. This is a good example of using SQL to make uncertainty visible.

slides.title: Standardize a Known Missing Representation
slides.transcript:
The null if function is very useful when one specific value should be treated as missing.

Here we trim spaces from the address. If the result is an empty string, the null if function returns null. Otherwise, it keeps the trimmed address.

[tts-break]

Suppose one record contains several spaces in the address field. Without trimming, the database technically sees a text value. After trimming, nothing remains, so we can represent that known blank state as null.

This is a reasonable transformation only when our rule says blank addresses should be considered missing.

Compare the original address with the normalized address. The point is not that null is always better than a blank. The point is that consistent missing-value representation makes later analysis and quality checks much easier.

slides.title: Use Fallback Values Carefully
slides.transcript:
Sometimes we want the first available value from several possible columns.

The coalesce function returns the first value that is not null. In this example, we first try a cleaned email address. If no usable email is available, we try the phone number. If neither is available, we return the phrase no contact method.

[tts-break]

Think of this as a fallback strategy, not a correction.

If a customer's email is missing and we use the phone number as the preferred contact, we have not repaired the email. We have only selected another available contact method.

That distinction matters because a fallback can be useful for a report or workflow while the original data quality problem still exists.

When you run the query, identify which records use email, which fall back to phone, and which have no available contact method.

slides.title: Standardization Is Different from Correcting a Fact
slides.transcript:
Not every transformation makes the same kind of claim.

If an email contains extra spaces and uppercase letters, trimming it and converting it to lowercase usually changes only the representation. We still believe it refers to the same email address.

If a business rule says the labels tech, electronic, and electronics all represent one category, mapping them to Electronics is also a documented standardization.

[tts-break]

But changing a negative price of negative fifty to positive fifty is different. Now we are claiming that we know the true price. That requires evidence.

A useful question is: am I changing how the same information is represented, or am I claiming that the underlying fact itself is different?

Standardize when equivalence is known. Correct a fact only when the correct value is supported by a trustworthy source or rule.

slides.title: Normalize Customer Names
slides.transcript:
Names often contain formatting differences that make analysis and matching harder.

The query starts by trimming spaces at the beginning and end of the name. It then uses a regular expression replacement to collapse repeated internal spaces into a single space. Finally, it applies consistent display capitalization.

[tts-break]

For example, imagine the source value contains several spaces before Jane, two spaces between Jane and Smith, and several spaces afterward. The cleaned representation becomes simply Jane Smith.

Notice what we are not doing. We are not deciding whether Jane Smith and Jane A. Smith are the same person. That would be an identity question.

Here we are only normalizing spacing and display case.

Run the query and compare the raw name with the cleaned name so you can see exactly what changed.

slides.title: Normalize Customer Emails
slides.transcript:
Email cleaning is another good example of safe representation changes.

The query trims spaces around the email, converts a blank result to null, and then converts the remaining text to lowercase.

For example, an email stored with spaces around it and uppercase letters can become a consistent lowercase value without changing the intended address.

[tts-break]

Why convert blank text to null? Because it gives us a consistent representation for a missing email and makes later filtering and counting easier.

But remember, lowercasing and trimming do not prove that the email actually exists. They only standardize the text.

Later, we will perform a structural validation check. Even that will only tell us whether the text looks like an email address, not whether messages can actually be delivered to it.

slides.title: Extract Phone Digits Before Validating
slides.transcript:
Phone numbers are often stored with parentheses, spaces, periods, dashes, or other formatting.

The first useful step is to separate normalization from validation.

The query removes every character that is not a digit. That gives us a digits-only version of the phone number. Then we ask whether the result has exactly ten digits.

[tts-break]

For example, a phone written as three three six, with punctuation around the area code and between the number groups, can normalize to the same ten digits as a phone written with only digits.

If the normalized value has ten digits, we keep it as a valid-shaped candidate. Otherwise, we return null for the validated field.

Again, ten digits do not prove that the number belongs to the customer. They only satisfy the technical rule we selected.

slides.title: Category Standardization Requires a Business Rule
slides.transcript:
Categorical values often contain several labels for what may be the same concept.

For example, a product dataset might contain electronics, electronic, and tech. We may want all three to appear as Electronics.

But SQL cannot know that these labels mean the same thing unless we define that rule.

[tts-break]

This is why category standardization is partly a business decision. The database can apply the mapping, but a person or organization must define what the mapping means.

Imagine another category called accessories. Should it be grouped with electronics? Maybe yes in one company and no in another.

So before creating mappings, review the observed values and document which source labels belong to each target category. Once that rule is clear, SQL can enforce it consistently.

slides.title: Use CASE for a Small Category Mapping
slides.transcript:
For a small number of category mappings, a case expression is easy to read and teach.

The query first handles missing or blank categories. Then it converts the source text to a consistent form and checks whether it belongs to one of several known groups.

For example, electronics, electronic, and tech are mapped to Electronics. Audio and headphones are mapped to Audio. Other known labels are handled in the same way.

[tts-break]

If a value does not match one of the documented groups, the query keeps it but gives it consistent capitalization.

This approach works well for a small teaching example. In a production system with many mappings, a separate lookup table is usually easier to maintain.

Run the query and compare the raw category with the standardized category. Focus on the idea that the mapping rule is explicit and reviewable.

slides.title: Detect Invalid Prices Before Correcting Them
slides.transcript:
Validation should normally happen before correction.

This query checks product prices and assigns a status. A missing price is labeled missing. A price less than or equal to zero is labeled invalid and marked for review. Anything else becomes a valid candidate.

[tts-break]

The important word again is candidate. A positive number satisfies our selected rule, but it may still be wrong. A product that normally costs twenty dollars could accidentally be entered as two thousand dollars and still pass this simple check.

Validation only tests the rules we define.

So begin with clear, transparent checks. Identify the records that fail. Then decide what to do with them based on evidence.

This is much safer than immediately changing every value that looks unusual.

slides.title: Validation Should Answer a Documented Question
slides.transcript:
A good validation rule should answer a specific question.

For an email, we might ask whether the cleaned text has the basic structure required by our system.

For a phone number, we might ask whether the normalized candidate contains the required number of digits.

For a price, we may ask whether a value is present and whether it falls inside an allowed numeric domain.

For stock quantity, we might require a nonnegative number.

[tts-break]

Notice that each check is tied to a documented expectation.

Avoid writing complicated validation logic just because you can. Start with the business question, then write the simplest SQL that tests that question.

A validation result is only meaningful when you can explain the rule behind it.

slides.title: Use a Regular Expression for Email Shape
slides.transcript:
A regular expression can help us test whether text follows a particular structure.

For the email example, we first handle missing or blank values. Then we test whether the cleaned email has a reasonable pattern: some text before the at sign, a domain after it, and a final domain ending.

[tts-break]

You do not need to memorize the full regular expression character by character. Focus on what it is doing: it is checking the shape of the text.

If the value matches, we label it valid shape. If it does not match, we label it for review.

But remember what this does not prove. An address can have a perfect shape and still be nonexistent, inactive, or typed for the wrong person.

Regular expressions are useful structural filters. They are not proof of real-world truth.

slides.title: Normalize Phone Numbers Before Checking Length
slides.transcript:
Phone validation becomes easier after normalization.

The query first removes punctuation and other non-digit characters. Then it checks the length of the resulting digit string.

If there are exactly ten digits, the phone receives a valid-shape status. If the original value is missing or blank, it is labeled missing. Other cases are sent for review.

[tts-break]

Imagine two phone values. One uses parentheses and a dash. The other contains exactly the same number with no punctuation. If we compare the raw strings, they look different. After digit extraction, they become identical.

That is why normalization should often happen before validation or matching.

When you run the query, inspect the original phone, the digits-only value, and the final status together.

slides.title: Combine Business Rules into a Row Status
slides.transcript:
Sometimes we want one status that summarizes the first problem found in a record.

This product-validation query checks several rules in order. It looks for a missing product name, a missing price, an invalid price, and a negative stock quantity. If none of those conditions is triggered, the row passes the selected rules.

[tts-break]

The order matters because a case expression returns the first matching condition.

For example, if a product has both a missing name and a negative price, this particular query reports the missing name first. That does not mean the price problem disappeared.

For a full data-quality system, we may want separate issue flags so multiple problems can be recorded at the same time.

Use this example to understand row-level validation, but also recognize its limitation: one status may summarize rather than capture every issue.

slides.title: Turn Row-Level Problems into Issue Counts
slides.transcript:
Once we can identify individual data-quality problems, we can summarize them.

This query creates a temporary issue list using a common table expression. One part identifies invalid customer emails. Another identifies invalid customer phone numbers. Another identifies invalid product prices.

The union all operation combines those issue records into one list.

[tts-break]

Then the final query groups by entity type and issue type and counts how many records have each problem.

Instead of reading the long SQL statement character by character, focus on the pattern: detect problems first, represent each problem as a row, then aggregate the issue rows.

This approach is useful for dashboards and monitoring. It can answer questions such as: what is our most common quality problem, and is that problem getting better or worse over time?

slides.title: Measure Quality Dimensions Separately
slides.transcript:
Data quality is not a single idea. It has several dimensions.

Completeness asks whether required values are present.

Validity asks whether values satisfy documented rules.

Uniqueness asks whether duplicate identities are controlled.

Timeliness asks whether the data is current enough for the intended use.

[tts-break]

A dataset can perform well in one dimension and poorly in another. For example, every customer may have a phone number, so completeness is high. But if many phone numbers are invalid, validity is low.

That is why it is useful to measure these dimensions separately before combining them into one overall score.

When someone says a dataset has ninety percent quality, ask what that number actually measures. A useful quality metric should be transparent enough that you can explain how it was calculated.

slides.title: Composite Quality Scores Are Policy Choices
slides.transcript:
Here we create a simple teaching example of a customer quality score.

The query checks four conditions: whether the name is present, whether the email has a valid shape, whether the phone has ten digits, and whether the signup date passes the selected date rule.

Each condition contributes twenty-five points, so a record can receive a score from zero to one hundred.

[tts-break]

The mathematics is simple, but the important question is why each check receives the same weight.

In a real organization, perhaps a valid email is more important than a phone number. Or perhaps the signup date should not affect quality at all.

So treat this score as an illustration, not a universal formula.

A composite score is a policy decision. Always keep the underlying component checks available so people can understand what the final number means.

slides.title: Summarize Quality Scores into Bands
slides.transcript:
After calculating a numeric quality score, we can summarize records into categories.

The query creates score bands such as Excellent, Good, Fair, and Poor, and then counts how many customers fall into each band.

This can make a quality report easier to read.

[tts-break]

But be careful not to hide too much information behind a label.

Suppose two customers both receive a score of seventy-five. One may be missing a phone number, while the other may have an invalid email. They have the same total score but different problems.

So quality bands are useful for high-level summaries, while the detailed issue flags remain important for action.

Use summaries to communicate. Use component-level checks to diagnose and improve the data.

slides.title: Find Duplicate Groups Before Choosing a Survivor
slides.transcript:
Deduplication should begin with detection, not deletion.

First, normalize the fields you plan to use as identity evidence. For example, convert emails to a consistent form and normalize name spacing and capitalization.

Second, group records using the duplicate key you have chosen.

Third, review groups where the count is greater than one.

[tts-break]

At this point, do not delete anything.

Two rows can look similar without representing the same person. Two family members might share a phone number. A person might use two email addresses. A common name can appear many times.

The goal of the first stage is to identify candidate duplicate groups.

Only after you understand the relationship should you decide whether records should be merged, ranked, quarantined, or simply left alone.

slides.title: Normalize Identity Fields Before Grouping
slides.transcript:
This query searches for duplicate groups using normalized email and normalized name.

The email is trimmed and converted to lowercase. The name has extra spaces removed and is given consistent display capitalization. Then the query groups records by those normalized values.

Only groups with more than one row are returned.

[tts-break]

The query also collects the source identifiers so you can see which records belong to the candidate group.

Imagine that one record contains Jane Smith with extra spaces and another contains the same name with different capitalization. Without normalization, SQL may treat them as different values. After normalization, they may fall into the same group.

That does not prove they are the same person. It gives us stronger evidence that the records deserve review.

slides.title: Different Duplicate Keys Answer Different Questions
slides.transcript:
The fields you use for duplicate detection change the meaning of the result.

Using normalized email alone is simple and often useful, but people can change emails, share accounts, or have missing values.

Using name plus email is more specific, but differences in spelling or missing information can split records that actually belong to the same person.

Phone digits can provide useful secondary evidence, but households may share a number and phone numbers can be reassigned.

[tts-break]

Combining several fields usually gives stronger evidence, but it also makes the logic more complex.

There is no perfect duplicate key for every dataset.

Choose identity evidence based on the domain, understand the risks of false matches and missed matches, and use human review when the consequences of an incorrect merge are important.

slides.title: Choose a Survivor with an Explicit Rule
slides.transcript:
After identifying a duplicate group, we may need to choose a preferred record, sometimes called the survivor.

That choice should follow an explicit rule.

One option is completeness: prefer the record with more useful populated fields.

Another is recency: prefer a newer trusted record when that makes sense.

A third is source priority: if one system is considered authoritative, prefer its record.

[tts-break]

And finally, use a stable tie-breaker, such as the record identifier, so the result is reproducible.

Imagine two duplicate records with the same name and email. One has a phone and address, while the other does not. A completeness rule may prefer the first record.

The key is that the decision should be explainable. We should never choose a survivor simply because one row happened to appear first.

slides.title: Use Row Number for Reproducible Ranking
slides.transcript:
The row number window function is useful when we need to rank duplicate candidates.

The query first calculates a completeness score. It gives a point when useful fields such as name, email, phone, or address are populated.

Then the duplicate records are grouped using the normalized identity fields.

Within each group, row number assigns a rank. More complete records come first. If completeness is tied, the query considers signup date, and then the identifier provides a stable final tie-breaker.

[tts-break]

The record with rank one is the preferred candidate according to this rule.

Notice that SQL is not deciding which person is real. We are implementing a policy that we designed.

Run the query and compare the completeness score with the survivor rank for the duplicate group.

slides.title: Some Possible Duplicates Need Review
slides.transcript:
Not every possible duplicate should be automatically merged.

This query compares customer records in pairs and looks for rows that share the same normalized phone number.

It uses a self join, meaning the customers table is joined to another copy of itself. The condition that the left identifier must be smaller than the right identifier prevents us from seeing the same pair twice.

[tts-break]

If two records share a phone number, the query returns their identifiers, names, and emails for comparison.

Suppose two customers have the same phone number but different names and emails. That could represent a duplicate, but it could also represent two people in the same household.

This is exactly the kind of situation where SQL should identify a candidate and a person may need to make the final decision.

slides.title: Separate Duplicate Detection from Resolution
slides.transcript:
Keep duplicate detection and duplicate resolution as two separate phases.

Detection asks: which rows might represent the same entity? It can use normalized keys, matching fields, or similarity evidence. Detection is often intentionally broad because we do not want to miss possible matches.

Resolution asks a different question: what should we do with those candidate records?

[tts-break]

Possible responses include selecting a survivor, merging selected fields, quarantining a group, or sending the records for manual review.

Resolution should usually be more conservative because it can change or consolidate data.

This separation gives you flexibility. You can improve your detection logic without automatically changing records, and you can apply different resolution policies depending on the risk and the business context.

slides.title: Quarantine Instead of Hiding Problems
slides.transcript:
When a record is questionable, one useful strategy is quarantine.

Quarantine does not necessarily mean moving the record to another physical database table. The main idea is to separate questionable data from trusted analytical data while preserving the source.

First, keep the original record.

Second, create issue flags that describe what is missing, invalid, or suspicious.

[tts-break]

Third, create a review subset containing only records that need attention.

Later, if evidence becomes available, those records can be corrected, approved, or promoted to a trusted layer.

For example, an invalid signup date should not be silently replaced with today's date. We can preserve the raw date text, produce a null cleaned date, and flag the record for review.

Quarantine makes uncertainty visible instead of pretending the problem has been solved.

slides.title: Expose Quality Issues with a View
slides.transcript:
A database view can expose quality problems without overwriting the source table.

The example creates a customer quality issues view. It keeps identifying fields such as customer ID, name, email, and phone, and then adds separate true-or-false flags.

One flag identifies a missing name. Another identifies an email that fails the selected shape check. Another identifies a phone that does not contain the required number of digits after normalization.

[tts-break]

The second query returns only records where at least one issue flag is true.

This design is useful because one customer can have more than one problem at the same time.

The source data stays intact, while the view gives us a reusable quality layer that can support review, reporting, or downstream cleaning workflows.

slides.title: Use Separate Raw, Clean, and Quality Layers
slides.transcript:
A strong data preparation design often keeps several logical layers.

The raw table preserves source records with little or no modification.

A clean view provides reusable transformations for analysis, such as normalized names, emails, and phone numbers.

A quality view exposes issue flags and review logic.

[tts-break]

Downstream users can then choose the layer appropriate for their task.

For example, an analyst building a dashboard may use the clean view. A data steward investigating problems may use the quality view. An auditor may need the raw table.

This layered approach is safer than repeatedly overwriting the same source columns.

It also makes your pipeline easier to explain: raw data came in here, standardization happened here, and quality rules were applied here.

slides.title: Create Clean Analytical Fields without Changing the Source
slides.transcript:
Here we create a clean preview view for the customers table.

The view standardizes the name, cleans the email, creates a ten-digit phone candidate when the number passes the selected rule, normalizes blank addresses, and keeps the signup date.

The original customers table is not changed.

[tts-break]

This is useful while developing cleaning logic because you can compare the clean preview with the source at any time.

Suppose you later decide that phone numbers should allow an international format. You can revise the view logic without trying to reconstruct values that were permanently overwritten.

Run the view and compare several rows with the original customers table.

A preview layer gives us a safe place to test analytical transformations before deciding whether any permanent correction is justified.

slides.title: Move Stable Rules Closer to Data Entry
slides.transcript:
Cleaning historical data is useful, but preventing future problems is even better.

Once a rule is stable and well understood, the database can help enforce it.

A not-null constraint can require a value.

A check constraint can enforce a domain or pattern rule.

A unique constraint can prevent duplicate values when uniqueness is truly required.

A foreign key protects relationships between tables.

[tts-break]

For example, if every order must reference an existing customer, a foreign key can prevent an order from pointing to a customer identifier that does not exist.

Constraints should represent rules we are confident about.

Do not use them to encode guesses. When a business rule is unclear, investigate first. When the rule becomes stable, move it closer to the point where data enters the system.

slides.title: Build a Small Validated Contact Table
slides.transcript:
This example creates a small contact table with several database constraints.

The contact identifier is the primary key. Email is required, so it uses a not-null rule.

A check constraint tests whether the email follows the selected structural pattern.

Another check requires the phone, when present, to contain exactly ten digits.

The email also has a unique constraint.

[tts-break]

The example then inserts one valid record.

After you run the valid insert, try changing one thing at a time. For example, use an email that does not follow the expected pattern, or use a phone with too few digits.

Postgres should reject values that violate the constraints.

This is how a database can prevent some known quality problems before they become part of the stored data.

slides.title: Do Not Add Strict Constraints Blindly
slides.transcript:
Constraints are powerful, but adding them to an existing database requires care.

First, profile the current data. You may discover that many historical records already violate the proposed rule.

Next, document allowed values and important exceptions.

Then decide how existing violations should be handled. Some may be corrected using evidence. Others may need to be quarantined or reviewed.

[tts-break]

Also consider the systems that insert data. A new constraint can break an existing import process if the incoming data does not satisfy the rule.

So the sequence matters: understand the data, confirm the business rule, address legacy problems, test the impact, and then enforce the stable rule.

Constraints are most effective when they are the final step of a well-understood quality policy, not the first reaction to messy data.

slides.title: Preview Before You Update
slides.transcript:
Permanent updates should follow a safe workflow.

Start with a select query that identifies exactly which rows would change.

Then begin a transaction.

Next, perform the update and use the returning feature so Postgres immediately shows the rows affected by the change.

Inspect the results carefully.

[tts-break]

If everything is correct, commit the transaction and keep the changes. If something is wrong, roll back the transaction and discard them.

Think of a transaction as a protected testing area for your update.

This is especially important when you are learning, working with production data, or applying a transformation to many rows.

A simple habit can prevent a serious mistake: select first, update inside a transaction, inspect the results, and only then decide whether to commit.

slides.title: Inspect a Reversible Cleaning Update
slides.transcript:
This example demonstrates a reversible update.

We begin a transaction, standardize customer emails by trimming spaces and converting the text to lowercase, and use returning to display the affected records.

The where condition limits the update to rows where the current email is actually different from the standardized version.

[tts-break]

Then the example performs a rollback.

That means you can see which rows would change, but the database does not keep the changes after the transaction ends.

This is an excellent way to test cleaning logic.

When you are confident that the transformation is correct and appropriate, the same workflow can end with commit instead of rollback.

While developing or teaching, rollback gives you a repeatable example because the source data remains unchanged.

slides.title: Compare Nullable Values Safely
slides.transcript:
Null values require special care in SQL comparisons.

If you compare a value with null using the normal equals operator, the result is not simply true or false. SQL treats the comparison as unknown.

That behavior can make update conditions difficult when nullable columns are involved.

[tts-break]

Postgres provides the phrase is distinct from. It gives us a null-safe way to ask whether two values are different.

For example, suppose we compare an existing email with a cleaned version. We want to know whether an update would actually change the value, even if one side could be null.

Using is distinct from makes that comparison explicit and predictable.

You do not need to use it everywhere, but it is a very useful Postgres feature when cleaning nullable data.

slides.title: Some Defects Should Stay Flagged
slides.transcript:
Some problems cannot be safely fixed automatically.

A negative price should not automatically become positive unless we know the intended value.

A bad date string should not be replaced with today's date simply to avoid a missing value.

A missing phone number should not be filled using some unrelated contact field.

And a possible duplicate should not be deleted simply because it has a lower identifier.

[tts-break]

The safer response is often to preserve the source, produce a cleaned value only when justified, and add a review status.

This may feel less satisfying because the dataset still contains unresolved problems. But that is actually more honest.

A clean dataset should not mean a dataset where uncertainty has been hidden. It should mean a dataset where known transformations are consistent and unresolved uncertainty is clearly represented.

slides.title: Record How Cleaning Decisions Were Made
slides.transcript:
Cleaning becomes much easier to audit when we record information about the process.

A source identifier tells us which raw record produced a cleaned row.

A rule version tells us which version of the cleaning logic was applied.

A cleaned-at timestamp tells us when the transformation ran.

Issue codes describe the quality problems detected.

And a review status tells us whether a record was accepted, rejected, or is still waiting for review.

[tts-break]

Imagine that a rule changes next month. If you stored the rule version, you can identify which records were processed with the older logic and decide whether they need to be reprocessed.

This kind of metadata turns cleaning from an informal one-time activity into a reproducible data pipeline.

slides.title: Project — Clean a Messy Staging Table
slides.transcript:
Now we will combine the ideas from the module into a small cleaning project.

The source is a messy customer staging table.

Our first task is normalization. We will standardize the representation of names, emails, and phone numbers.

Next, we will parse signup dates, but only for date formats that we explicitly support.

Then we will rank possible duplicate records using a reproducible rule.

Finally, we will label each output row as either a candidate clean row or a row that needs review.

[tts-break]

The goal is important: we are not trying to create a magically perfect source table.

We are creating a candidate-clean analytical output while preserving uncertainty and making our decisions visible.

This is much closer to how a real data preparation workflow should behave.

slides.title: Read the Full Cleaning Pipeline as Stages
slides.transcript:
The query here is long, so do not try to read every symbol from beginning to end.

Instead, read it as a sequence of stages.

The first common table expression is called normalized. It cleans the basic text representations while keeping the raw date string.

The next stage is called typed. It attempts to convert only supported date formats into real date values.

The third stage is called ranked. It calculates duplicate ranking using normalized identity fields and a completeness rule.

[tts-break]

Finally, the outer query returns cleaned analytical fields and assigns a row status.

This is one reason common table expressions are useful: they let us break a complex cleaning pipeline into understandable steps.

Run the whole query once. Then use the next few slides to study each stage separately.

slides.title: Normalize Without Guessing
slides.transcript:
The first stage creates normalized versions of the messy customer fields.

For the name, we trim surrounding spaces, collapse repeated internal spaces, and convert an empty result to null.

For the email, we trim the text, convert it to lowercase, and convert a blank to null.

For the phone, we keep only digits. If no digits remain, the result becomes null.

[tts-break]

The signup date is different. At this stage, we preserve the original date text exactly as it came from the source.

Why? Because date parsing is a separate decision.

Keeping normalization and parsing separate makes the pipeline easier to understand and debug.

Each stage should do one clear job. That way, if a value looks wrong later, we can trace where the change occurred.

slides.title: Parse Only Supported Date Formats
slides.transcript:
Date parsing is a good place to be conservative.

In the project, we support two known formats.

The first is year, month, day, such as 2026 dash 10 dash 22. When the source matches that structure, we convert it to a date.

The second is month, day, year, using slashes. When the text matches that format, we use the documented conversion rule.

[tts-break]

What happens when the source value uses some other format or contains an impossible date? We return null rather than inventing a date.

For example, if the source contains text that could be interpreted in two different ways, guessing could silently create the wrong date.

A null cleaned date plus a review flag is safer than a confident but incorrect value.

slides.title: Rank Duplicate Candidates Reproducibly
slides.transcript:
The ranking stage groups records using normalized email and normalized name.

Within each candidate duplicate group, it calculates how complete each record is. A usable name, email, valid-shaped phone, and parsed signup date each contribute to that completeness logic.

The more complete record is ranked first.

[tts-break]

If two records have the same completeness, the identifier is used as a stable tie-breaker.

That final tie-breaker matters because it makes the result deterministic. If you run the query again on the same data, you should receive the same ranking.

Remember that rank one means preferred by our selected policy. It does not prove that the record is factually superior in every possible way.

The ranking is a reproducible decision rule, not a statement of absolute truth.

slides.title: Return Clean Fields and a Review Status
slides.transcript:
The final project output contains both cleaned fields and information about uncertainty.

Clean name is the normalized display version of the name.

Clean email is the normalized email candidate.

Clean phone is only kept when the normalized number contains the expected ten digits.

Signup date clean contains a real date only when the source matched one of the supported formats.

Duplicate rank indicates the record's position inside a candidate duplicate group.

[tts-break]

The row status tells us whether the record passes the selected technical checks or should be reviewed.

This is a useful output design because it does not hide the cleaning logic.

An analyst can use the clean fields, while the duplicate rank and status still communicate where additional attention may be needed.

slides.title: A Clean Candidate Is Not Verified Truth
slides.transcript:
A record labeled candidate clean has passed the technical checks selected for this exercise.

That is useful, but it does not mean every value has been verified against the real world.

A review status means the record contains missing, invalid, unsupported, or unresolved information.

The duplicate rank helps us compare candidate records, but it does not prove identity.

[tts-break]

For example, an email can have a valid structure, a phone can have ten digits, and a date can parse correctly, yet the information can still belong to the wrong person.

Technical validation improves consistency. It does not automatically establish truth.

That distinction is one of the most important professional habits in data work: describe exactly what your checks prove, and do not claim more than the evidence supports.

slides.title: Explain the Cleaning Decisions
slides.transcript:
Before moving on, make sure you can explain the reasoning behind the techniques we used.

Why are null and blank text different? Because null represents the absence of an SQL value, while a blank is still a stored text value.

Why do we flag an invalid numeric value before correcting it? Because knowing that a value is wrong does not tell us the correct replacement.

[tts-break]

Why do we separate duplicate detection from survivor selection? Because identifying possible matches and deciding what to do with them are different decisions.

What does a regular expression prove? Only that text matches the selected structure.

And why test updates with returning and rollback? Because we can inspect the proposed changes before permanently keeping them.

If you can explain these ideas in your own words, you understand the logic behind the SQL rather than only the syntax.

slides.title: Assessment — Build a Clean Output without Overwriting the Source
slides.transcript:
For the assessment, you will build a cleaned customer output while leaving the source table unchanged.

The starter query gives you the original customer fields inside a common table expression.

Your task is to extend that query.

Create a cleaned name by handling spacing and display case. Create a cleaned email by trimming and standardizing the text. Create a cleaned phone candidate using the rules from this module.

[tts-break]

Then add a row-level quality status and a duplicate rank.

As you work, think about the order of operations. Normalize before you validate. Detect possible duplicates before making any resolution decision. Preserve uncertainty instead of inventing replacements.

Do not focus only on making the query run. Make sure you can explain why each transformation is appropriate.

slides.title: Cleaning Habits to Keep
slides.transcript:
There are several habits from this module that I want you to keep using.

Profile first. Measure the data before changing it.

Preserve uncertainty. Do not invent values just because a field is missing or invalid.

Keep standardization, validation, duplicate detection, and correction conceptually separate.

Use safe layers such as views, review sets, and transactions so the original evidence remains available.

[tts-break]

Add constraints only after the rule is stable and existing problems are understood.

And when you measure data quality, keep the individual dimensions visible even if you also calculate one summary score.

These habits make your SQL more than technically correct. They make your data preparation process safer, more reproducible, and easier for someone else to understand.

slides.title: Choose the Response Based on the Evidence
slides.transcript:
Different data-quality problems require different responses.

If two values differ only in formatting and we know they mean the same thing, standardize the representation.

If a documented rule says blank text means missing, normalize it to null.

If a value violates a rule but the true value is unknown, flag it or quarantine it rather than guessing.

[tts-break]

If records may represent the same entity, detect the candidate group and then apply a ranking or review process.

If an authoritative source supports a correction, update the data safely and keep an audit trail.

And when a rule is stable for future data, enforce it with a constraint or ingestion validation.

The main lesson is simple: the evidence should determine the action.

slides.title: Next Module — Reshaping Data
slides.transcript:
You have now completed the main data-cleaning workflow for this course.

You learned how to profile messy data, distinguish different missing states, standardize text, validate values, measure quality, identify duplicate candidates, preserve questionable records for review, use constraints, and test updates safely.

These skills give us something very important: a more trustworthy and explainable dataset.

[tts-break]

In the next module, we will build on that foundation by reshaping data.

A clean relational table is not always in the best shape for analysis. Sometimes we need a wide format. Sometimes we need a long format. We may need to pivot categories into columns, unpivot columns into rows, or change the analytical grain.

So the next question becomes: once the data is clean, how should we organize it for reporting, comparison, visualization, and modeling?

That is where we will continue in Module 10.
